# Assembling the Compendium {#sec-zzcollab}

A collaborator clones your repository, runs the analysis script,
and gets a p-value of 0.06 where your draft reports 0.04. Nothing
errors. Over two days the two of you find three differences: her
R packages are a year newer than yours, the cleaned dataset in
the repository was produced by a version of the cleaning script
you have since edited, and one exclusion was made by hand in a
spreadsheet that never entered the repository. Each difference is
a piece of the study that did not travel with the code. Pin the
packages and the same rerun can still differ: if the repository
could not hold the outcomes file and the README said to copy it
from a shared drive that now holds a later, corrected extract,
nothing in the repository could tell either of you that the
inputs differed. A research compendium is the arrangement in
which everything needed to produce the paper, from the raw data
to the environment, lives in one directory with a layout a
stranger can read, and the Five Pillars are the checklist that
says every layer the answer depends on is pinned. This chapter
sets out what a compendium is and where its files go, then
assembles the pillars, builds the result, and audits it, so that
the collaborator's rerun either matches or tells you why not.

::: {.bookepigraph}

\begin{flushright}\small
```

container for the different elements that make up the
document and its computations (i.e. text, code, data, ...),
and as a means for
distributing, managing and updating the collection.*

[Robert Gentleman and Duncan Temple Lang]{.smallcaps},
*Statistical Analyses and Reproducible Research* (2007)

```

## What a research compendium is {#sec-rrtools}

A paper without its compendium is a description of an analysis;
a compendium without a paper is code. Together they are a study
artifact that survives the loss of any individual file, and of any
individual person. Gentleman and Temple Lang
[-@gentleman2007statistical] introduced the term, and Marwick,
Boettiger, and Mullen [-@marwick2018packaging] gave the working
definition this book uses, which has three criteria:

| Criterion | What it requires | What fails without it |
|---|---|---|
| Single directory | Code, data, environment, and narrative together | A step lives elsewhere (a spreadsheet, a laptop), as the hand exclusion in the opening did |
| Computable | Another user can rerun the analysis with reasonable effort | The paper can be read but not checked |
| Self-describing | The layout follows a convention a stranger knows | Every file is a hunt, for the stranger and for you in eighteen months |

: The three criteria for a research compendium. {#tbl-rrtools-criteria}

The argument for convention is practical. A directory organized
to your own logic is navigable by you and by nobody else, and
'nobody else' includes the version of you that returns after
eighteen months. A compendium that follows a recognized layout
can be opened by a stranger who has seen one before: they will
know where the paper is, where the raw data are, and which
directory holds things that were derived rather than given. The
specific convention matters much less than having one at all.

R packages already have a convention every R user knows
(`DESCRIPTION`, `R/`, `man/`), which satisfies the third
criterion and part of the first. What a package lacks is a study:
data and a paper. The `rrtools` package [@marwick2018rrtools]
supplies one convention that adds them, and @fig-compendium-anatomy
shows the result.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-compendium-anatomy
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart. A research compendium branches into three
%%|   components: a package backbone of DESCRIPTION, R/ and man/;
%%|   an analysis directory holding data, paper and figures; and a
%%|   Dockerfile with renv.lock. Each leads in turn to the property
%%|   it supplies: self-describing so a stranger can navigate it, a
%%|   single directory holding code, data and narrative together,
%%|   and computable so another user can re-run it."
%%| fig-cap: "What a compendium is made of. The package backbone
%%|   supplies convention and dependency declaration; the analysis
%%|   directory supplies the study; the Dockerfile supplies the
%%|   environment. Remove any of the three and the reader loses
%%|   navigability, content, or the ability to run it."
flowchart TD
  C["Research compendium"]
  C --> P["<b>Package backbone</b><br/>DESCRIPTION, R/, man/<br/><i>convention and dependencies</i>"]
  C --> A["<b>analysis/</b><br/>data/, paper/, figures/<br/><i>the study itself</i>"]
  C --> D["<b>Dockerfile + renv.lock</b><br/><i>the environment</i>"]
  P --> N["<i>self-describing</i><br/>a stranger can navigate it"]
  A --> S["<i>single directory</i><br/>code, data, narrative together"]
  D --> R["<i>computable</i><br/>another user can re-run it"]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does `rrtools` reuse the R package structure
instead of inventing a new layout?

**Answer.** Three practical reasons. The package structure is the
only widely recognized layout in the R ecosystem, so the
compendium is navigable for free. The package gives dependency
declaration: `DESCRIPTION` lists what the code needs, and `renv`
(@sec-renv) pins the versions. And it gives function management:
helpers in `R/` are documented, tested, and loadable into the
analysis. The cost is a few package files that are not used as a
package (no CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network, submission,
no users importing it), which is small against the structural
payoff.
:::

## Where files go {#sec-rrtools-layout}

### The layout

`rrtools` produces the layout below; most compendium conventions
differ from it only in names.

```
readmissions/
├── DESCRIPTION
├── NAMESPACE
├── R/                       # reusable functions
├── man/
├── analysis/
│   ├── data/
│   │   ├── raw_data/
│   │   └── derived_data/
│   ├── figures/
│   ├── paper/
│   │   ├── paper.qmd
│   │   └── references.bib
│   └── supplementary-materials/
├── Dockerfile
├── data-manifest.sha256
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
├── README.qmd
├── README.md
└── readmissions.Rproj
```

| Path | Holds | Commit it? |
|---|---|---|
| `R/` | Reusable functions: cleaning helpers, plotting wrappers, model utilities, documented with roxygen | Yes |
| `analysis/data/raw_data/` | The data exactly as received, never edited | If small and unrestricted; otherwise document the access path |
| `analysis/data/derived_data/` | Everything the scripts produce from the raw data | Optional: commit when small and the analysis is archived |
| `analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | The manuscript, with the code that produces its numbers | Yes |
| `analysis/figures/` | Figures the analysis writes | Usually not; the code that makes them is committed |
| `analysis/supplementary-materials/` | Appendix tables, sensitivity analyses | Yes |
| `data-manifest.sha256` | One checksum per raw file | Yes, always, even when the raw data cannot be committed |
| `README.qmd` | What the project is, how to build it in one command, where the paper and data are, how to cite it | Yes |

: Where each file goes. {#tbl-rrtools-layout}

The README is the entry point, not the documentation: it says what
the project is, how to rebuild it, and where things are. Long
technical notes live elsewhere.

### Raw data are read-only

Raw and derived data live in separate directories because raw
data are evidence and derived data are a build product. Writing a
cleaned table back over the input destroys the only copy of what
you were given, and version control does not recover a file that
was overwritten before it was ever committed. Treat `raw_data/` as
read-only, by convention if your file system will not enforce it,
and make the convention checkable: record a checksum of every raw
file when it arrives. The chunk below builds the layout above in a
temporary directory and copies in two of the HF-HOME raw files.

```{r}
#| label: rrtools-toy-compendium
comp <- file.path(tempdir(), "readmissions")
layout <- c("R", "analysis/data/raw_data", "analysis/data/derived_data",
            "analysis/paper", "analysis/figures")
purrr::walk(file.path(comp, layout), dir.create, recursive = TRUE,
            showWarnings = FALSE)

hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
raw_dir <- file.path(comp, "analysis", "data", "raw_data")
file.copy(file.path(hf_dir, c("randomization.csv", "outcomes.csv")),
          raw_dir, overwrite = TRUE)
```

The manifest is one line per file: the file's SHA-256 checksum (a
64-character fingerprint of its contents) and its path from the
compendium root, in the format the `shasum` command reads and
writes, so that you can create it in R and anyone can check it
from a shell.

```{r}
#| label: rrtools-manifest
raw_files <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$")
sums <- vapply(file.path(raw_dir, raw_files), cli::hash_file_sha256,
               character(1))
writeLines(paste0(sums, "  ",
                  file.path("analysis", "data", "raw_data", raw_files)),
           file.path(comp, "data-manifest.sha256"))
readLines(file.path(comp, "data-manifest.sha256"))

check_raw <- function(root) {
  lines <- readLines(file.path(root, "data-manifest.sha256"))
  recorded <- setNames(sub("  .*$", "", lines),
                       sub("^\\S+  ", "", lines))
  current <- vapply(file.path(root, names(recorded)),
                    cli::hash_file_sha256, character(1))
  changed <- names(recorded)[unname(current) != recorded]
  if (length(changed) > 0) {
    stop("raw data changed since the manifest: ",
         paste(changed, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}
check_raw(comp)
```

From the compendium root, `shasum -a 256 --check
data-manifest.sha256` checks the same manifest from the shell. A
checksum detects accidental change, which is the job here; it is
not a defense against deliberate tampering, since whoever can edit
the data can edit the manifest beside them.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A 'quick fix' saved over the raw export leaves no trace in the
data.** Exclude a few patients by hand and save the file in place,
and every later run reads the edited file as if it were what the
site sent:

```{r}
#| label: rrtools-manifest-pitfall
#| error: true
outcomes_path <- file.path(raw_dir, "outcomes.csv")
outcomes <- read.csv(outcomes_path,
                     colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
write.csv(outcomes[-(1:3), ], outcomes_path, row.names = FALSE)
check_raw(comp)
```

The analysis would have run, on
`r format(nrow(outcomes) - 3, big.mark = ',')` patients instead of
`r format(nrow(outcomes), big.mark = ',')`, with no error. The
manifest makes it loud. Exclusions belong in code, in
`derived_data/`, where they are counted and reviewed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your cleaning script reads
`analysis/data/raw_data/visits.csv` and produces a tidy analytic
table. Where does the output go, and should it be committed?

**Answer.** It goes in `analysis/data/derived_data/`, and whether
to commit it is a trade-off, not a rule. Against committing: it is
reproducible from the raw data and the script, so storing it
duplicates information and adds a binary that changes on every
run. For committing: it lets a reader check your numbers without
installing your environment, and it fixes what the analysis
actually used, which matters if the cleaning script is later
corrected. The usual resolution is to commit derived data when it
is small and the analysis is being archived, and to leave it
untracked during development. What is not defensible is committing
derived data and *not* the script that made it, which is the
arrangement that looks tidiest and explains least, and the one
behind the opening's stale dataset.
:::

### Exercises

1. Assign each file from a messy project to the layout of
   @tbl-rrtools-layout: `helpers.R` (three functions used by two
   scripts), `crf_export_2025-06-01.csv` (from the data center),
   `analytic.rds` (written by `clean.R`), `fig2.png`, `notes.txt`
   (a dated log of decisions), `clean.R`, and `manuscript.qmd`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
| File | Goes to | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `helpers.R` | `R/` | Reused by more than one script |
| `crf_export_2025-06-01.csv` | `analysis/data/raw_data/` | Received, not produced; add it to the manifest |
| `analytic.rds` | `analysis/data/derived_data/` | Produced by a script; regenerable |
| `fig2.png` | `analysis/figures/` (usually untracked) | Produced by code |
| `notes.txt` | Top level or `analysis/` as a decision log | Not data and not code; keep it with the project and in Git |
| `clean.R` | `analysis/` (scripts) | Study-specific code that turns raw into derived data |
| `manuscript.qmd` | `analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | The manuscript |

The judgment calls are `notes.txt`, which fits no category and
should not be forced into one, and `clean.R`, which some
conventions put in `analysis/scripts/`. What matters is that a
stranger can predict the location.
:::

## The Five Pillars {#sec-zzcollab-pillars}

The three criteria say what a compendium must achieve, and the
layout says where its files go. The Five Pillars say what it must
contain to achieve them. The preceding chapters each solved one
layer of the reproducibility problem and each left the wiring to
you. A compendium layout does not come with a lockfile; a lockfile
(@sec-renv) does not come with a container; a container
(@sec-docker) does not know where your data came from. The Five
Pillars are the checklist that says when the wiring is complete.
They are tool-neutral roles: the book uses the R tools for each,
but every language has a tool for each role, and the same five
hold whether you assemble them by hand or let a framework do it.
@tbl-five-pillars states what each pins and what goes wrong
without it.

| Pillar | Pins | In this book | Elsewhere | Without it | Check |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Dockerfile | Operating system, system libraries, the R build | `Dockerfile` (@sec-docker) | Apptainer definition, Nix | Packages restore onto a different R or BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms), and the last digits of an estimate move | The base image's R version equals the lockfile's |
| 2. `renv.lock` | The exact version and source of every R package | `renv.lock` (@sec-renv) | `uv.lock`, conda `environment.yml` | A collaborator's newer packages, or a changed default in one, change a number without an error | `renv::status()` reports no issues |
| 3. `.Rprofile` | Activation of the project library at startup | `.Rprofile` (@sec-renv) | A virtual-environment activation script | R loads the global library instead, and the lockfile is silently bypassed | `.libPaths()[1]` is inside `renv/library` where you render |
| 4. Source code | Every step, from raw data to every number | `R/` and `analysis/` in Git (@sec-git-solo) | Any version-controlled scripts | A hand step or an edited script is not in the history, or nobody can identify the version that ran | Committed to Git, and the submitted version tagged |
| 5. Data | The raw inputs, unchanged, or the documented way to get them | `analysis/data/raw_data/` with a checksum manifest | A DOI'd deposit with access instructions | A stale derived file or a later extract gives a different answer from the same code | A committed checksum manifest verifies |

: The Five Pillars as a tool-neutral checklist. Each is necessary;
none is sufficient, and a compendium missing any one is
incomplete. {#tbl-five-pillars}

The opening's three causes map onto pillars 2, 4, and 5. The
remedy for each is not care but a file: a lockfile, a script for
every step, and raw data that the code reads and never writes.
Some frameworks automate the pillars; `zzcollab`
(@sec-zzcollab-optional) is one, and it scaffolds and audits all
five.

The pillars are easier to remember as a stack than as a list,
because each one captures a layer the one above it takes for
granted. @fig-five-pillars is that stack.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-five-pillars
%%| fig-alt: "Five layers stacked bottom to top, each depending on
%%|   the one below. From the bottom: the Dockerfile supplying
%%|   operating system, system libraries and the R build; renv.lock
%%|   pinning every R package version; .Rprofile activating the
%%|   project library; the source code in R/ and analysis/; and at
%%|   the top the data, raw and derived or a documented path to
%%|   it."
%%| fig-cap: "The Five Pillars as a layered stack. Each layer
%%|   assumes the one beneath it. Remove the Dockerfile and the R
%%|   packages have no operating system to install onto; remove the
%%|   lockfile and the source code has no packages; remove the data
%%|   and there is nothing to analyze."
flowchart TD
  D["<b>5. Data</b><br/><i>raw and derived, or a documented path to them</i>"]
  S["<b>4. Source code</b><br/><i>the analysis, in R/ and analysis/</i>"]
  P["<b>3. .Rprofile</b><br/><i>activates the project library</i>"]
  L["<b>2. renv.lock</b><br/><i>every R package version</i>"]
  F["<b>1. Dockerfile</b><br/><i>operating system, system libraries, R build</i>"]
  F --> L --> P --> S --> D
```

Two of the pillars need a word more than the table gives them.
The `renv.lock` records the R version as well as every package,
but it does not install R; the R installation comes from the
Dockerfile, which is why the two must agree. And the data pillar
does not require the data to be in the repository. Sensitive data
often cannot live in the compendium; then the compendium holds a
README documenting the access path, in the form @sec-federal sets
out, and a manifest of checksums that lets anyone confirm they
obtained the same files. The shared-drive variant of the opening
was a data pillar with the README and without the manifest.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A project has a Dockerfile and a committed
`renv.lock`, and its `.Rprofile` activates `renv`. Which pillars
does a collaborator still have to take on trust?

**Answer.** Two. The source code is pinned only if it is
committed and the version you reported is tagged; otherwise the
collaborator cannot know which commit produced the paper. And the
data are pinned only if they are in the repository or a manifest
records their checksums; otherwise a later extract produces a
different answer from the same code, with nothing to say so. The
environment pillars cannot detect either problem.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your compendium has a `renv.lock` and a Dockerfile.
A colleague argues that the lockfile is redundant, because the
image already contains the packages. Is it?

**Answer.** No. The image contains the packages that were current
when it was built, and a rebuild months later installs whatever
is current then, unless the lockfile pins them; the Dockerfile's
restore step reads the lockfile for exactly that reason. The
pillars are a stack, not a menu: the Dockerfile pins what is
beneath R, and the lockfile pins what is above it.
:::

### Exercises

2. A repository contains `analysis.R`, `clean.R`, `data.csv`
   (described in the README as 'cleaned'), `renv.lock`, and a
   README that says 'run analysis.R in RStudio'. Which pillars are
   present, which are missing, and what would a collaborator's
   rerun be unable to establish?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Present: package versions (`renv.lock`) and source code, assuming
the repository is under Git. Missing: the environment beneath R
(no Dockerfile, so R and system libraries are whatever the
collaborator has), activation (no `.Rprofile`, so the lockfile is
ignored unless she restores it by hand), and the raw data. The
data pillar is the serious gap: `data.csv` is derived, so a rerun
can check `analysis.R` against it but can never check `clean.R`,
and any hand step between the raw export and `data.csv` is
invisible. Add the raw export (or its access path), make
`clean.R` read it and write to `derived_data/`, and record a
checksum manifest.
:::

## Assembling the compendium by hand {#sec-zzcollab-assemble}

Assembling the pillars by hand takes about half an hour per
project, and doing it once is the best way to understand what any
framework that automates it is doing for you. Each step uses a
tool from an earlier chapter; the commands below are
display-only, because they create a project on your machine.

1. **Layout and source code.** Scaffold the compendium with
   `rrtools` (@sec-rrtools-scaffold) and put it under Git
   (@sec-git-solo):

   ```r
   rrtools::use_compendium("~/research/hfhome")
   rrtools::use_analysis()
   ```

   ```bash
   git init
   ```

2. **Lockfile and `.Rprofile`.** Initialize `renv`, which writes
   both, install what the analysis uses, and snapshot
   (@sec-renv):

   ```r
   renv::init()
   renv::snapshot()
   ```

3. **Dockerfile.** Copy the canonical Dockerfile from
   @sec-docker-canonical to the project root, with its
   `.dockerignore`, and set the base image's tag to the R version
   in `renv.lock`. Use it in place of the one
   `rrtools::use_dockerfile()` writes (@sec-rrtools-scaffold).

4. **Data.** Put the raw files in `analysis/data/raw_data/`, or a
   README there that says how to obtain them, and commit a
   checksum manifest of the files (@sec-rrtools-layout).

5. **Tag.** Commit, and tag the commit you submit:

   ```bash
   git tag -a v1.0-submission -m "Submitted to journal"
   ```

### Scaffolding with `rrtools` {#sec-rrtools-scaffold}

The calls below are display-only, because they create a project
and open it as a new RStudio session:

```r
# install
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("benmarwick/rrtools")

# create a new compendium
rrtools::use_compendium("~/research/readmissions")
# (this also runs usethis::create_package internally)

# add the analysis directories
rrtools::use_analysis()

# add a Dockerfile and, by default, a GitHub Actions
# workflow that renders the paper inside it
rrtools::use_dockerfile()

# add a README.qmd
rrtools::use_readme_qmd()
```

`rrtools::use_dockerfile()` writes its own Dockerfile, based on
`rocker/verse`. This book replaces it with the canonical Dockerfile
in @sec-rrtools-build, so that this chapter, @sec-renv, and
@sec-docker describe one file rather than several.

### Other conventions

`rrtools` is one convention among several, and the right one
depends on the project's shape and the team's habits:

| Convention | Shape | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `rrtools` | R package plus `analysis/` | A paper with reusable R code; the default for a biostatistical paper |
| Quarto manuscript project | A Quarto project whose output is an article | A paper-first project without a package backbone |
| Quarto book | A Quarto project with chapters | Book-length output, such as this practicum |
| A framework such as `zzcollab` (@sec-zzcollab-optional) | Scaffolds all five pillars and audits them | You want the pillars generated and checked for you |
| The TIER Protocol (Teaching Integrity in Empirical Research) | A documented folder convention | Social-science collaborators who already use it |
| Your group's template | Whatever the group agreed | Always, if one exists: consistency with colleagues beats any external default |

: Compendium conventions. {#tbl-rrtools-conventions}

Defaulting to `rrtools` is reasonable; defaulting to it without
thought is not.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to propose a layout for an existing project, and apply
the moves yourself.

> **Context.** Below is the output of `git ls-files` for an R
> analysis project, and the compendium layout I want (the table of
> paths and contents). The working tree is clean and committed.
>
> **Constraints.** Propose only `git mv` commands. Do not move,
> rename, or edit anything under `data/raw/`; raw files keep their
> names and contents, and are moved, if at all, only into
> `analysis/data/raw_data/` with a separate command I will run
> myself. Delete nothing. Do not edit file contents.
>
> **Criteria.** Every file is assigned exactly once. List the
> files that fit no category, with your reasoning, rather than
> forcing them into one, and list every script whose file paths
> will break after the moves.

*Failure mode.* A model assigns every file somewhere, confidently,
including logs and exploratory notebooks that fit nowhere, and
proposes edits to paths inside scripts that silently change what
they read. Raw files moved or renamed lose the link to their
provenance. *Check.* After applying the moves, `git status` and
`git diff -M --name-status HEAD` should show only renames (`R100`),
no modifications or deletions; `shasum -a 256 --check
data-manifest.sha256`, rerun after the manifest's paths are updated
to the new locations, should pass; and a fresh render should
produce the same numbers. The prompt sends file names, not data
(@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### The paper inside the compendium {#sec-rrtools-paper}

`analysis/paper/paper.qmd` is the manuscript, written in Quarto
(@sec-quarto): code chunks for the analyses, inline numbers,
figure cross-references, and citations from `references.bib`.

````qmd
---
title: "Effect of post-discharge home health visits on 30-day readmission"
author:
  - name: A. Author
  - name: B. Coauthor
format:
  pdf: default
  html: default
bibliography: references.bib
---

# Methods

We analyzed `{{r}} nrow(d)` patients from the institutional
EHR cohort. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause
readmission and the exposure was receipt of a home-health
visit. We fit a multivariable logistic regression
adjusting for age, sex, baseline ejection fraction, and
discharge medications, in R [@rcore2024].

```{{r}}
#| label: fit-model
#| echo: false
fit <- glm(readmit ~ home_health + age + sex + ef + meds,
           family = binomial, data = d)
ci <- exp(confint.default(fit)["home_health", ])
```

The adjusted odds ratio for home-health-visit receipt
was `{{r}} round(exp(coef(fit)["home_health"]), 2)` (95% CI
`{{r}} round(ci[1], 2)` to `{{r}} round(ci[2], 2)`).
````

Every number in the methods and results comes from code, so a
rerun on corrected data changes the prose with the tables. EHR
here is the electronic health record; the example is an
observational cohort, which is why the exposure is receipt of a
visit and the estimate is adjusted.

For journal-specific formatting in Quarto, use a Quarto journal
extension where one exists for your journal. The `quarto-journals`
collection on GitHub includes, for example, a template for JASA
(the *Journal of the American Statistical Association*):

```bash
quarto use template quarto-journals/jasa
```

The extension adds a format (here `jasa-pdf`) that you name under
`format:` in `paper.qmd`. The older `rticles` package offers more
journals, including *Statistics in Medicine*, *Biometrics*, and
JASA (`rticles::journals()` lists them), but its templates are R
Markdown output formats for an `.Rmd` file rendered with
`rmarkdown::render()`, not Quarto formats; they cannot be named in
the `format:` key of a `.qmd`. Neither collection has a template
for every medical journal (there is none for NEJM or JAMA, for
instance), and most of those journals accept a plain PDF or Word
manuscript at first submission.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Render the paper in a fresh session and read the warnings, which
are where unresolved citations and cross-references surface:

```bash
quarto render analysis/paper/paper.qmd 2>&1 | grep -i warn
```

It should print nothing. A warning that a citation or a
cross-reference cannot be resolved means the rendered paper shows
a placeholder where a reference belongs.
:::

### A compendium with two gaps

The manifest is the step most projects skip. The chunk below
assembles a small HF-HOME compendium in a temporary directory,
with the manifest step deliberately left out and a Dockerfile
copied from an older project, so that the audit in
@sec-zzcollab-audit has something to find.

```{r}
#| label: zzcollab-toy-compendium
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
comp <- file.path(tempdir(), "hfhome-compendium")
unlink(comp, recursive = TRUE)
raw <- file.path(comp, "analysis", "data", "raw_data")
dir.create(raw, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(file.path(comp, "R"))
invisible(file.copy(
  file.path(hf_dir, c("randomization.csv", "outcomes.csv")), raw
))
writeLines(
  "derive_analysis_set <- function(rand, outc) merge(rand, outc)",
  file.path(comp, "R", "derive.R")
)
writeLines('source("renv/activate.R")', file.path(comp, ".Rprofile"))
writeLines(
  '{"R": {"Version": "4.4.0", "Repositories": []}, "Packages": {}}',
  file.path(comp, "renv.lock")
)
writeLines(c("FROM rocker/r-ver:4.3.1", "WORKDIR /work"),
           file.path(comp, "Dockerfile"))
invisible(system2("git", c("init", "-q", comp)))
list.files(comp, recursive = TRUE, all.files = TRUE,
           include.dirs = FALSE) |>
  grep(pattern = "^[.]git/", invert = TRUE, value = TRUE)
```

Every pillar has a file. Whether every pillar is *pinned* is a
different question, and the listing cannot answer it.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**An `.Rprofile` that never runs.** R reads `.Rprofile` from the
directory it starts in, then from your home directory. Render from
a subdirectory (`cd analysis/paper`, or an RStudio project rooted
there) and the project's `.Rprofile` at the root never runs: no
error, no message, and the analysis uses your global library while
the lockfile says otherwise. This book hit exactly this, because
Quarto starts R in the directory being rendered; its fix is a
second `.Rprofile` in `analysis/report/` that points `renv` at the
project root. The check in @tbl-five-pillars catches it: run
`.libPaths()[1]` from the directory where you render.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Step 3 sets the Dockerfile's base tag to the R
version in `renv.lock`. What happens if the two disagree, and why
is nothing likely to report it?

**Answer.** `renv` restores the recorded package versions onto
whatever R the image supplies. The build usually succeeds, because
most package versions install on a neighboring R, and the analysis
runs. What changes is the layer beneath the packages (R itself,
and the numerical libraries it links), so results can differ in
their last digits from the ones you reported, with no error
anywhere.
:::

## Building and sharing {#sec-rrtools-build}

A compendium is built in one of three ways: render the paper in
RStudio while writing; source the analysis scripts in order after
`devtools::load_all()` to regenerate cached results; or build the
image, which is the only one that reproduces the environment as
well as the results. The book's canonical Dockerfile, explained
line by line in @sec-docker-canonical, sits at the compendium
root:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.4.0

ARG QUARTO_VERSION=1.6.40

RUN apt-get update \
  && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    ca-certificates curl \
    libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev libuv1-dev \
  && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# rocker/r-ver ships R but not the Quarto CLI
RUN arch="$(dpkg --print-architecture)" \
  && curl -fsSL -o /tmp/quarto.deb \
    "https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v${QUARTO_VERSION}/quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${arch}.deb" \
  && dpkg -i /tmp/quarto.deb \
  && rm /tmp/quarto.deb

# outside /work, so a bind mount of the project cannot hide it
ENV RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library

WORKDIR /work
COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./
COPY renv/activate.R renv/activate.R
RUN R -q -e "renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)"

COPY . .

CMD ["quarto", "render", "analysis/paper/paper.qmd"]
```

From the compendium root (display-only):

```bash
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t readmissions:v1.0 .
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$(pwd)/analysis/paper:/work/analysis/paper" \
  readmissions:v1.0
```

The Dockerfile pins the R version, the system libraries, and
(through `renv.lock`) the package versions, and the rendered paper
appears in `analysis/paper/` on your machine. A reader with Docker
can rebuild a very close copy of the environment that produced the
paper; an exact copy needs the digest pin or archived image
described in @sec-docker.

Deposition is treated in full in @sec-federal. Its shape affects
how you organize the directory, so it is worth knowing now: GitHub
(or your institution's Git server) holds the working repository;
an archive such as Zenodo holds a citable, DOI-bearing (digital
object identifier) snapshot at submission, with the saved image;
and restricted primary data go only where the data use agreement
permits, often a controlled-access repository and sometimes
nowhere, with the compendium documenting how to request them.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
The test of a compendium is a rebuild by someone who is not you,
from what is in the repository and nothing else. Simulate it
(display-only):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/you/readmissions.git /tmp/fresh
cd /tmp/fresh
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t readmissions:check .
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$(pwd)/analysis/paper:/work/analysis/paper" readmissions:check
```

The paper must render, and its key numbers must match yours. A
failure here names a file that lives only on your machine, which
is the opening's problem found before your collaborator finds it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why is the fresh clone the right test, rather than
rendering the paper again on your own machine?

**Answer.** Your machine has everything the repository forgot: the
packages you installed, the derived files you never committed, the
environment variables in your `.Renviron`. A rerun there passes
whatever the compendium is missing. A fresh clone, built in a
container, has only what the five pillars supply, so it is the
first run that can fail for the reasons a collaborator's would.
:::

### Exercises

3. A colleague's compendium renders on her laptop and fails in the
   fresh-clone check with `cannot open file
   'analysis/data/derived_data/analytic.rds'`. What is the likely
   cause, and what are the two acceptable fixes?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The paper reads a derived file that exists on her disk and is not
in the repository, probably because `derived_data/` is listed in
`.gitignore` and nothing in the build regenerates it. Either make
the build produce it (the paper, or a script the Dockerfile's
command runs, calls the cleaning code on the raw data), which is
the better fix because it also tests the cleaning; or commit the
derived file together with the script that made it, which is
acceptable for an archived analysis. Committing it without the
script is the arrangement the layout Check warned against.
:::

## Worked example: a small compendium {#sec-rrtools-worked}

A simulation study set up as a compendium from scratch
(display-only):

```r
# scaffold; this opens the new compendium as its own
# RStudio project, and every later call runs in that
# session, whose working directory is the compendium
rrtools::use_compendium("~/research/sim2026")

rrtools::use_analysis()
rrtools::use_readme_qmd()

# the environment pillars: initialize renv, then replace
# rrtools's Dockerfile with the canonical one
renv::init()

# add the simulation function
usethis::use_r("simulate")
# (write R/simulate.R with a documented function)
devtools::document()

# add the paper
file.edit("analysis/paper/paper.qmd")
# (write the manuscript using simulate() from the package)

# render
quarto::quarto_render("analysis/paper/paper.qmd")

# version control
usethis::use_git()
usethis::use_github(private = TRUE)
```

Then snapshot, commit, and tag the milestone from the shell, in
the compendium directory:

```bash
Rscript -e 'renv::snapshot()'
git add .
git commit -m "Initial compendium"
git tag -a v0.1-draft -m "Initial draft for PI review"
```

The compendium is now a self-contained directory with
package-style code, a paper that uses the code, a lockfile and a
Dockerfile that pin the environment, a Git history, and a tag at a
meaningful milestone. The setup takes about thirty minutes.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the pillars are committed and the tree is clean:

```bash
git ls-files Dockerfile renv.lock .Rprofile analysis/paper/paper.qmd
git status --short
git tag -l 'v0.1*'
```

The first command should list all four files, the second should
print nothing, and the third should print `v0.1-draft`. Then run
the fresh-clone check of @sec-rrtools-build against the tag.
:::

## Auditing the pillars {#sec-zzcollab-audit}

A checklist you run by eye drifts; a checklist you run as code
does not. The function below turns @tbl-five-pillars into five
assertions about a project directory. It uses only `renv`, `cli`,
and base R, so it audits a compendium however it was assembled.

```{r}
#| label: zzcollab-audit-fn
audit_pillars <- function(root) {
  path <- function(...) file.path(root, ...)
  lock_r <- if (file.exists(path("renv.lock"))) {
    renv::lockfile_read(path("renv.lock"))$R$Version
  } else {
    NA_character_
  }
  from <- if (file.exists(path("Dockerfile"))) {
    grep("^FROM ", readLines(path("Dockerfile")), value = TRUE)[1]
  } else {
    NA_character_
  }
  rprofile <- if (file.exists(path(".Rprofile"))) {
    readLines(path(".Rprofile"))
  } else {
    character(0)
  }
  code <- list.files(root, pattern = "[.](R|qmd|Rmd)$",
                     recursive = TRUE)
  manifest <- path("data-manifest.sha256")
  data_ok <- file.exists(manifest) && {
    m <- read.table(manifest, col.names = c("sha256", "file"))
    all(vapply(path(m$file), cli::hash_file_sha256, character(1)) ==
          m$sha256)
  }
  data.frame(
    pillar = c("Dockerfile", "renv.lock", ".Rprofile",
               "Source code", "Data"),
    check = c("base image tag equals the lockfile's R version",
              "lockfile present and readable",
              "activates renv",
              "analysis code present, under Git",
              "raw files match the checksum manifest"),
    ok = c(
      !is.na(from) && !is.na(lock_r) &&
        grepl(paste0(":", lock_r, "($|@)"), from),
      !is.na(lock_r),
      any(grepl("renv/activate.R", rprofile, fixed = TRUE)),
      length(code) > 0 && file.exists(path(".git")),
      data_ok
    )
  )
}

audit_pillars(comp)
```

Two pillars fail. The Dockerfile names R 4.3.1 while the lockfile
records 4.4.0, and there is no manifest for the data. Fix both:
set the base tag to the lockfile's version, and write the
manifest.

```{r}
#| label: zzcollab-audit-fix
lock_r <- renv::lockfile_read(file.path(comp, "renv.lock"))$R$Version
writeLines(c(paste0("FROM rocker/r-ver:", lock_r), "WORKDIR /work"),
           file.path(comp, "Dockerfile"))

data_files <- list.files(raw, full.names = TRUE)
writeLines(
  paste0(vapply(data_files, cli::hash_file_sha256, character(1)),
         "  ", file.path("analysis", "data", "raw_data",
                         basename(data_files))),
  file.path(comp, "data-manifest.sha256")
)

audit <- audit_pillars(comp)
audit
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Assert the audit rather than reading it, and confirm from a shell
that the manifest is in the standard format (display-only; run it
in the compendium's root):

```{r}
#| label: zzcollab-audit-verify
stopifnot(all(audit$ok))
```

```bash
shasum -a 256 --check data-manifest.sha256
```

The shell check prints `OK` beside each file. In your own project,
run `audit_pillars(".")` from the root before every tag, and
regenerate the manifest only when you deliberately receive new
data, committing it with the data change. For a project under Git,
`git ls-files Dockerfile renv.lock .Rprofile` confirms that the
files are committed, not merely present on your disk.
:::

The audit is a structural check. It confirms that each pillar is
present and consistent; it finds what is missing, and it cannot
tell you that what is present works or that the analysis
reproduces. That test is the rebuild from a fresh clone in
@sec-rrtools-build: build the image, restore the lockfile, run the
analysis, and compare the results with the ones you reported.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
A model can map an unfamiliar project onto the pillars quickly.
Give it the files that decide each pillar, not a description.

> **Context.** Below are the output of
> `git ls-files` for an R analysis project, the `FROM` line of its
> Dockerfile, the `R$Version` from its `renv.lock`, and the full
> text of its `.Rprofile`.
>
> **Constraints.** Assess the Five Pillars (Dockerfile,
> `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, source code, data) using only these
> inputs. Do not recommend a framework or a template. Do not
> propose moving or editing anything in the raw-data directory.
>
> **Criteria.** For each pillar: present, absent, or present but
> inert, with the line of input that shows it. For each gap, the
> smallest addition that closes it.

*Failure mode.* Models report a pillar as present because a file
with the right name exists: an `.Rprofile` that never activates
`renv`, a Dockerfile whose tag disagrees with the lockfile, a data
README with no checksums. Or they recommend adopting a framework,
which answers a different question. *Check.* Run `audit_pillars()`
on the project and compare its `ok` column with the model's
verdicts. File names and configuration are structure; send no
data files (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The audit passes on your compendium. A month later a
colleague edits one value in `outcomes.csv` to correct a data
entry error and reruns the analysis. What does the audit report,
and what should happen next?

**Answer.** The data pillar fails, because the file's checksum no
longer matches the manifest. That is the audit doing its job: the
inputs changed, and now someone knows. Raw data are evidence, so
the correction should arrive as a new extract with its provenance
recorded, the manifest regenerated and committed with it, and the
changed result explained, not as a hand edit to the file.
:::

### Exercises

4. In the toy compendium, change one outcome in
   `analysis/data/raw_data/outcomes.csv` and rerun the audit.
   Which pillar fails?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-10-4
outcomes_path <- file.path(raw, "outcomes.csv")
lines <- readLines(outcomes_path)
lines[2] <- sub(",0,", ",1,", lines[2], fixed = TRUE)
writeLines(lines, outcomes_path)
audit_pillars(comp)[c("pillar", "ok")]
```

Only the data pillar fails. A one-character change to one patient
is invisible to every other check, and to anyone reading the
results; the manifest is what makes it loud.
:::

5. Audit this book's own repository with
   `audit_pillars(file.path("..", ".."))` and explain each failure.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-10-5
audit_pillars(file.path("..", ".."))[c("pillar", "ok")]
```

Each `FALSE` is a pillar the book's repository does not supply in
the form the audit checks. A missing Dockerfile means the R
version and system libraries are whatever the reader's machine
has; a missing data manifest means the reader cannot confirm the
files match the ones the book was built from, though here the
HF-HOME files can be regenerated from their seeded script. A book
that teaches the pillars is held to them too.
:::

## Choosing how much to automate {#sec-zzcollab-choosing}

Assembling by hand gives you full control and costs half an hour
per project. It is also exactly the kind of work that gets done
slightly differently every time, which defeats the consistency it
was supposed to produce. Alfred North Whitehead observed, in *An
Introduction to Mathematics* (1911), that 'civilization advances
by extending the number of important operations which we can
perform without thinking about them'; the tools below make the
assembly one such operation. They automate parts of it, and they
differ in which pillars they supply and in how much of the layout
they decide for you.

| Approach | Supplies | Leaves to you | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| By hand | Whatever you choose, as above | Every step, and its consistency across projects | Learning the pillars; a single paper |
| `rrtools` [@marwick2018packaging] | Package-style layout, a Dockerfile, a README | The lockfile, matching the Dockerfile to it, the data manifest | A paper with code, in the community-standard layout |
| `workflowr` [@blischak2019workflowr] | A project website in which each results page records its Git commit and R session information | The lockfile, the container, the data manifest | An analysis that is shared as it develops, as a website |
| `zzcollab` (@sec-zzcollab-optional) | Layout, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, Dockerfile, a `Makefile`, dependency checks | The data manifest's upkeep, and the choice of profile | A group producing many projects that should look alike |

: Ways to assemble a compendium. None removes the audit.
{#tbl-zzcollab-approaches}

The right level of infrastructure is itself a judgment. Excessive
infrastructure on a small project is busywork; insufficient
infrastructure on a large one is technical debt. A compendium is
overkill for interactive exploration, for a one-off script, for a
teaching example whose point is the code, and for a quick
reproduction of someone else's analysis, whose structure should
control. It is the right weight for a collaborative analysis
passed between team members, for one that must survive months or
years after its lead analyst has moved on, and for any analysis
subject to the federal requirements of @sec-federal. A tool that
makes the heavy path cheap moves the right answer toward more
infrastructure on the margin, but never removes the need to
decide.

Whichever path you take, the group's conventions (a preferred
database client, a set of in-house packages, a journal's Quarto
template) are best written down once, in a template project or a
shared lockfile, so that every new project inherits them rather
than re-enumerating them.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague argues that adopting a framework makes
the pillar audit unnecessary, since the framework writes every
file. What is wrong with the argument?

**Answer.** A framework writes the pillars once, at scaffolding
time; the audit checks them now. Lockfiles drift as packages are
installed, a Dockerfile's base tag falls behind a lockfile
snapshotted under a newer R, and data change after the manifest is
written. Each failure in @tbl-five-pillars can occur in a
scaffolded project as easily as in a hand-built one.
:::

### Exercises

6. For each project below, choose an approach from
   @tbl-zzcollab-approaches and name the pillar you would check
   most often: (a) a one-off descriptive table for a clinician's
   abstract; (b) a two-year trial analysis passed between three
   analysts; (c) a methods paper with a simulation study.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) A script, with no compendium; if the abstract becomes a paper,
promote it then. (b) A framework that makes every project in the
group look alike, `zzcollab` or a group template, with the data
pillar checked most often, because extracts arrive throughout the
trial. (c) `rrtools` or a hand-built compendium; the pillar to
watch is the environment (Dockerfile and lockfile together),
because simulation results depend on the random-number generator
and numerical libraries. Other defensible answers exist; the
reasoning should tie the approach to the project's lifetime and
number of hands.
:::

## Optional: automating the assembly with zzcollab {#sec-zzcollab-optional}

This section is optional. `zzcollab` is the author's in-house
framework (@sec-lab-software), one way to automate the assembly
beside `rrtools` and `workflowr`; nothing else in the book
depends on it. It packages the ideas of `rrtools`, `renv`, and
Docker into one command-line workflow, trading control over the
layout for speed of setup and uniformity across a group's
projects. It does not call `rrtools`; it writes its own layout,
modeled on the same compendium.[^zzcollab-version]

[^zzcollab-version]: Described as of the repository at
    `github.com/rgt47/zzcollab` in October 2026. Profiles, `make`
    targets, and the bundle schema have changed between versions;
    check the repository's `CHANGELOG.md` and `make help` before
    relying on the details below.

### The first-project walkthrough

The minimum `zzcollab` session (display-only):

```bash
mkdir hfhome-analysis
cd hfhome-analysis
zzc tidyverse             # scaffold (Five Pillars appear)
make r                    # enter R session inside Docker
                          # ... do analysis ...
make check-renv           # validate dependencies
make docker-render-qmd    # render the Quarto report
```

**`zzc tidyverse`** runs the framework's
scaffolding. After it completes, the directory
contains a `DESCRIPTION`, `R/`, `analysis/`, and
`tests/` directories, a Quarto report at
`analysis/report/index.qmd`, a minimal `renv.lock`, a
`Dockerfile` on the `rocker/tidyverse` base, and a
`Makefile`. It then offers to build the image. Git is
a separate step (`zzc git`, or `git init` yourself).
The generated Dockerfile pins the rocker base image by tag and,
when Docker can resolve it, by digest (for example
`rocker/r-ver:4.6.0@sha256:...`).

**`make r`** drops you into an interactive R session
inside the container, with the project directory
mounted, so files edited inside the container persist
on the host. It does not build the image; if no image
exists it asks whether to run R on the host instead,
defaulting to No, so an unbuilt image stops you rather
than silently substituting the host's R. Build first with
`make docker-build` if you declined at scaffolding time.

**`make check-renv`** runs
`zzrenvcheck::check_packages(auto_fix = TRUE,
strict = TRUE)` on the host; the first time it runs it
installs `zzrenvcheck` itself from the latest commit on
GitHub, unpinned. It checks that the packages your code
uses and the packages `DESCRIPTION` declares agree, and,
separately, that `DESCRIPTION` and `renv.lock` agree; by
default it does not follow indirect dependencies, so
passing this check is not the same as `renv::status()`
reporting no issues (@sec-renv). With `auto_fix` it
*edits* `DESCRIPTION` and `renv.lock` to add what is
missing, which can take two runs: the first pass adds a
package to `DESCRIPTION`, and the lockfile update follows
on the next. It is not a read-only audit; use
`make check-renv-no-fix` for a report that changes
nothing. It does not build the Dockerfile or inspect
`.Rprofile` or the data.

**`make docker-render-qmd`** runs
`quarto render analysis/report/index.qmd` inside the
container. (`make docker-render` renders an R Markdown
report instead, `analysis/report/report.Rmd` by
default.)

### The project `Makefile`

Every `zzcollab` project gets a `Makefile` with many targets;
`make help` lists them. The ones used most:

| Target | Action |
|---|---|
| `make help` | List all targets |
| `make r` | Drop into R inside the project's container |
| `make rstudio` | Launch RStudio Server (port 8787) |
| `make docker-render-qmd` | Render `analysis/report/index.qmd` in the container |
| `make check-renv` | Validate dependencies and add missing ones |
| `make check-renv-no-fix` | Validate dependencies without modifying files |
| `make snapshot` | Snapshot `renv.lock` in the container, then validate |
| `make docker-build` | Rebuild the image (use after adding packages) |
| `make hash-data` | Write a SHA-256 manifest of the raw-data directory |
| `make verify-data` | Check the raw data against that manifest |
| `make clean` | Remove package build artifacts |

: Common `zzcollab` `make` targets. {#tbl-zzcollab-make}

`make hash-data` writes `data-manifest.sha256` in the same
`shasum` format as the manifest in @sec-zzcollab-audit, so
`audit_pillars()` reads either. `make docker-build` rebuilds the
image after you add packages or system dependencies; `make r`
silently uses the old image until you do. `make clean` removes
package build artifacts (`*.tar.gz` and `*.Rcheck`); it does not
touch rendered reports or Quarto's `_freeze/` directory.

`make rstudio` is for browser-based work. Open
`http://localhost:8787` and log in as `rstudio` with the password
`rstudio`, which the target prints. The target publishes port
8787 on all of your machine's network interfaces, so with that
fixed password, use it only on a trusted network (see
@sec-docker for binding to `127.0.0.1` instead).

### Choosing a profile

The command `zzc <profile>`, run inside an empty project
directory, scaffolds a project using one of four profiles, and a
profile's main job is to choose the rocker base image:

| Profile | Base image | Approximate size | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `minimal` | `rocker/r-ver` | 650 MB | Command-line work, continuous integration |
| `tidyverse` | `rocker/tidyverse` | 1.2 GB | Tidyverse data analysis |
| `rstudio` | `rocker/rstudio` | 980 MB | RStudio Server development |
| `publishing` | `rocker/verse` | 4.2 GB | Manuscripts that need LaTeX |

: `zzcollab` profiles. {#tbl-zzcollab-profiles}

The `tidyverse` profile was formerly called `analysis`, and
`zzc analysis` still works as a deprecated alias. There are no
modeling or Shiny profiles; for those needs the framework's own
advice is to start from one of the four and add packages inside
the container. The profile is a substantive choice: a manuscript
that must render to PDF needs LaTeX, which only the `publishing`
profile's base image has, while a simple descriptive analysis in
the `publishing` profile waits for a 4 GB image it does not need.

Modeling packages need no special profile. Install
`lme4` or `survival` inside the container, record them
with `make snapshot`, and rebuild with
`make docker-build`. When zzcollab generates the
Dockerfile it reads the packages your code, `DESCRIPTION`,
and `renv.lock` mention and adds the system libraries
they need, so a profile mismatch costs a rebuild rather
than a hand-edited `apt-get` line.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You are scaffolding a project that will fit a Cox
proportional hazards model with `survival::coxph()` and a
mixed-effects model with `lme4::glmer()`, then render the result
as a PDF manuscript. Which profile?

**Answer.** `publishing`, because the PDF manuscript is the one
requirement a profile actually supplies: it is the only profile
whose base image includes LaTeX. The modeling packages are not a
profile question at all. Install `lme4` and `survival` inside the
container, run `make snapshot` so that `renv.lock` and
`DESCRIPTION` record them, and rebuild. Neither package needs an
extra system library; `survival` is a recommended package that
ships with R.
:::

### Bundles and extension

Profiles are defined in the repository's
`templates/bundles.yaml`, which has three sections:
`library_bundles` name sets of system packages, `package_bundles`
name sets of R packages, and `profiles` combine a base image with
one bundle of each. There is no `inherits` key, and the quickstart
command accepts only the four built-in profile names. A group that
wants different defaults can add a profile entry in a fork and
select it with `zzc docker --profile <name>`, but the Dockerfile
generator reads only the entry's `base_image`; system libraries
come from the packages the project uses, and R packages are added
inside the container and recorded with `make snapshot`. Group
conventions therefore belong in a template project or a shared
`renv.lock`, as for any other approach, not in a new profile.

### Exercises

7. Scaffold a `zzcollab` project in a scratch directory, copy the
   two HF-HOME files into `analysis/data/raw_data/`, run
   `make hash-data`, and audit the result with `audit_pillars()`.
   (This needs Docker and the `zzc` command, and creates a project
   on your machine.)

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A complete scaffold passes every row except, until you commit, the
source-code row's Git check (`zzc git` or `git init`). If the
Dockerfile row fails, compare its `FROM` line with the lockfile's
`R$Version`: the two were written at different times, and the fix
is to rebuild with `make docker-build` after a snapshot, not to
edit the tag by hand. Run `make check-renv-no-fix` as well; unlike
`make check-renv`, it changes nothing.
:::

## Analysis code as a package, without zzcollab {#sec-zzcollab-diy-package}

`zzc tidyverse` writes a `DESCRIPTION`, an `R/` directory, and a
Dockerfile in one command, but none of what makes that backbone
*useful* is specific to `zzcollab`, or to `rrtools`, or to any
framework. A function documented with `roxygen2`, checked with
`R CMD check`, and loadable by name instead of by `source()` is
ordinary R package development, available to a repository that
uses no framework at all. This section does that development by
hand on one function from this chapter's own examples, so that the
choice to adopt a scaffolding tool is a choice about convenience,
not about whether the pillar it writes for you is reachable
without it.

The function is the composite-outcome derivation the rest of this
book writes inline wherever it needs HF-HOME's primary endpoint:
30-day readmission or death, with the outcome set to missing when
the patient was never ascertained.

```{r}
#| label: zzcollab-diy-function
derive_composite_outcome <- function(outcomes) {
  outcomes |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      composite_30d = dplyr::if_else(ascertained,
                                     as.integer(event_30d),
                                     NA_integer_)
    )
}

outcomes <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"),
  col_types = readr::cols(patient_id = "c", .default = "?")
)
composite <- derive_composite_outcome(outcomes)
c(events = sum(composite$composite_30d, na.rm = TRUE),
  unascertained = sum(is.na(composite$composite_30d)))
```

Written this way, in a script, the function is reused by copying
it (and silently diverging) into every script that needs it, it is
documented only by whatever comment sits above it, and nothing
checks that its argument or return value still match what a caller
assumes six months later. Turning it into a package function fixes
all three, and every step below is ordinary R, not a `zzcollab`
feature.

### A minimal `DESCRIPTION` by hand

A package needs a `DESCRIPTION` file at its root; `usethis` and
`rrtools` write one for you, but the file itself is nine lines of
plain text, no different from one you type:

```
Package: hfhome
Title: Analysis Functions for the HF-HOME Trial
Version: 0.1.0
Authors@R: person("A", "Author", email = "a@example.org",
    role = c("aut", "cre"))
Description: Derivation and summary functions for the HF-HOME
    home-health trial analysis.
License: MIT + file LICENSE
Imports: dplyr
Encoding: UTF-8
```

`Imports:` is the field that matters most and is easiest to let
drift: every package a function in `R/` calls with `::` belongs
here, and `R CMD check` (below) is what notices when it does not.
Nothing about this file depends on a scaffolding tool; a text
editor and the fields `devtools::create()` would have written are
enough.

### Documenting with `roxygen2`

`roxygen2` [@wickham2024roxygen2] turns a comment block directly
above a function into its help page, keeping the documentation and
the code in the file a reader already has open instead of in a
separate `.Rd` file that drifts out of sync. The block below would
sit above `derive_composite_outcome()` in `R/derive.R` (display-only;
it edits a package source tree that does not exist on this
machine):

```r
#' Derive the HF-HOME composite outcome
#'
#' Sets the 30-day composite outcome (readmission or death) to
#' missing for patients whose outcome was never ascertained.
#'
#' @param outcomes A data frame with logical column `ascertained`
#'   and integer column `event_30d`.
#' @return `outcomes` with an added integer column `composite_30d`.
#' @examples
#' derive_composite_outcome(
#'   data.frame(ascertained = c(TRUE, FALSE), event_30d = c(1, 0))
#' )
#' @export
derive_composite_outcome <- function(outcomes) {
  outcomes |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      composite_30d = dplyr::if_else(ascertained,
                                     as.integer(event_30d),
                                     NA_integer_)
    )
}
```

Running `devtools::document()` reads every such block in `R/` and
writes `man/derive_composite_outcome.Rd` and the `export()` lines
in `NAMESPACE`; nobody edits either file directly (display-only):

```r
devtools::document()
#> Writing NAMESPACE
#> Writing derive_composite_outcome.Rd
```

The payoff is not cosmetic. `?derive_composite_outcome` now works
from any script that loads the package, the `@examples` block is
code that can be run (and, in `R CMD check`, is run), and a
function whose documented `@param` no longer matches its signature
is something the next step catches rather than something a reader
discovers by trial and error.

### Checking the package

`R CMD check`, run through `devtools::check()`, is what `roxygen2`
comments alone cannot give you: a battery of structural tests
against the whole package, not just the one function you are
looking at (display-only; it requires the package tree and is not
installed in this environment):

```r
devtools::check()
#> ── R CMD check results ──────────────────────── hfhome 0.1.0 ────
#> Duration: 4.1s
#>
#> ❯ checking Rd \usage sections ... WARNING
#>   Argument items with no description in Rd object
#>   'derive_composite_outcome':
#>     'outcomes'
#>
#> 0 errors ✔ | 1 warning ✖ | 0 notes ✔
```

The warning above is deliberately left in to show what the check
is for: it would have caught a `@param` line typed for the wrong
argument name, which no amount of careful reading of the function
body would. `R CMD check` also verifies that every package named
after `::` in `R/` is declared in `Imports:`, that the examples run
without error, that the `NAMESPACE` matches what `roxygen2` wrote,
and that the package installs cleanly in a fresh session; none of
this is a `zzcollab` or `rrtools` feature, because it is the same
check CRAN runs on every submission, available to any package
whether or not it is ever submitted.

### Optional: a browsable site with `pkgdown`

`pkgdown` [@wickham2024pkgdown] renders every `man/*.Rd` page,
along with the `README`, into a static website, which is worth the
one extra command when more than one person reads the functions
(display-only):

```r
pkgdown::build_site()
# or, to publish it automatically on every push:
usethis::use_pkgdown_github_pages()
```

For a one-author analysis this is usually not worth the setup; for
a package that a team imports across several studies, a site that
`?derive_composite_outcome` cannot show in a chat message is often
what gets it actually read.

@tbl-zzcollab-diy-vs-framework lines up what each layer costs
against what it buys, continuing the comparison of
@tbl-zzcollab-approaches.

| Step | By hand | Automated by `rrtools` / `zzcollab` |
|---|---|---|
| `DESCRIPTION` fields | Typed once, about five minutes | Scaffolded with placeholders you still edit |
| `roxygen2` comment content | Always yours to write | Never automated; no tool knows what a function does |
| `NAMESPACE` and `man/*.Rd` | `devtools::document()`, one command either way | Same command; not framework-specific |
| `R CMD check` | `devtools::check()`, one command either way | Same command; not framework-specific |
| `pkgdown` site | `pkgdown::build_site()`, one command either way | Same command; not framework-specific |
| Deciding *to* package the code at all | Your judgment | Your judgment; no framework makes this call |

: What turning analysis code into a package costs, with or without
a scaffolding tool. The commands in the last four rows are
identical either way; what a framework actually saves is the first
row and the file layout around it. {#tbl-zzcollab-diy-vs-framework}

The practical reading of the table is that `rrtools` and
`zzcollab` save you the `DESCRIPTION` boilerplate and the decision
about where files go, and nothing more. The work that makes a
package worth having, writing the documentation and reading what
the check reports, is the same work with or without them, and it
is the work most worth learning by hand once, as @sec-zzcollab-assemble
argued for the pillars generally.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague says there is no point documenting
`derive_composite_outcome()` with `roxygen2` unless the package is
going on CRAN. Is that right?

**Answer.** No. `roxygen2` and `R CMD check` are useful to any
package, submitted anywhere or nowhere; CRAN runs the same check
because it is a good check, not because CRAN invented it. An
in-house package that only two analysts ever install still benefits
from `?derive_composite_outcome` working, from the check catching a
`@param` that drifted from the signature, and from the examples
block running as a test every time `devtools::check()` runs. CRAN
submission adds a few more checks (URLs, spelling, package size);
it does not add the value of documenting and checking in the first
place.
:::

### Exercises

8. Add a second function to the toy package above,
   `readmission_rate(composite)`, that returns the proportion of
   non-missing `composite_30d` values equal to 1. Write its
   `roxygen2` block, including an `@examples` line that would run
   under `R CMD check`, and say which `Imports:` entry, if any, it
   adds to `DESCRIPTION`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-10-8
readmission_rate <- function(composite) {
  mean(composite == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
}
readmission_rate(composite$composite_30d)
```

```r
#' Readmission or death rate among ascertained patients
#'
#' @param composite An integer vector of composite-outcome values,
#'   as returned by [derive_composite_outcome()].
#' @return A single proportion between 0 and 1.
#' @examples
#' readmission_rate(c(1, 0, 0, NA))
#' @export
readmission_rate <- function(composite) {
  mean(composite == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
}
```

It adds nothing to `Imports:`: `mean()` and the comparison
operator are base R, and the function never calls another package
with `::`. The example line uses a vector with a missing value on
purpose, so the check exercises the same `na.rm = TRUE` branch the
real data uses.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 1: the compendium is the unit.** Code, data,
   environment, and paper travel together in one directory with a
   convention a stranger knows; audit all five pillars, not the
   ones a tool happens to write, and tag what you submit, because
   the fresh clone of that tag is the test.
2. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence; derived data are a build
   product.** Never write to `raw_data/`, commit a checksum
   manifest and change it only when new data arrive deliberately,
   and regenerate everything else from code.
3. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** The lockfile and the
   Dockerfile pin different layers, and they must agree on the
   R version.

## Cumulative practice

9. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-solo, @sec-quarto, @sec-renv, and
   @sec-docker).* Assemble by hand a compendium for a small
   HF-HOME analysis: the `rrtools` layout, with
   `randomization.csv` and `outcomes.csv` in
   `analysis/data/raw_data/` and a checksum manifest; a
   `paper.qmd` that reports the 30-day event proportion in each
   arm with inline code; `renv` with a snapshot; and the canonical
   Dockerfile with its tag set from the lockfile. Commit and tag
   `v0.1`. Run `audit_pillars()` until every row passes, then
   build the image and render the paper inside it from a fresh
   clone.
10. *On your own work (no key).* Convert a 'scripts and data'
   project of your own into a compendium, documenting the location
   of every file and the reason for it. Audit it with
   `audit_pillars()`, record for each failing pillar what it would
   take to close it and whether you think it is worth it, and
   record what the fresh-clone check found the first time you ran
   it.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
9. The paper's numbers come from the raw files, never typed. A
   minimal computing chunk:

```{r}
#| label: soln-10-9
rand <- read.csv(file.path(raw_dir, "randomization.csv"),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
outc <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
hf <- merge(rand[c("patient_id", "arm")],
            outc[c("patient_id", "event_30d")], by = "patient_id")
stopifnot(nrow(hf) == nrow(rand))
round(100 * tapply(hf$event_30d, hf$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
```

The chunk reads `outcomes.csv` from the HF-HOME directory, because
the Pitfall in @sec-rrtools-layout edited the toy compendium's
copy; in your compendium, both files come from `raw_data/`, and
`check_raw()` runs first. If the audit's Dockerfile row fails, the
base tag and the lockfile's R version disagree; set the tag from
`renv::lockfile_read("renv.lock")$R$Version`. A passing audit is
still a structural check; the fresh-clone render is the test.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Command or file | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Scaffold a compendium | `rrtools::use_compendium()`, `use_analysis()` | An improvised layout |
| Pin what is beneath R | The canonical Dockerfile (@sec-docker-canonical); base tag equals `renv::lockfile_read("renv.lock")$R$Version` | A different R or system library |
| Pin the packages | `renv::init()`, `renv::snapshot()`; check with `renv::status()` | Newer packages on a collaborator's machine |
| Activate the project library | `.Rprofile`, written by `renv::init()`; check `.libPaths()[1]` from the render directory | A lockfile silently bypassed |
| Protect raw data | `data-manifest.sha256`, from `cli::hash_file_sha256()` or `make hash-data`; `shasum -a 256 --check data-manifest.sha256` | Edits saved over the raw export; a later extract |
| Audit the pillars | `audit_pillars(".")`; `git ls-files` | A pillar missing, inert, or not committed |
| Render the paper | `quarto render analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | Typed numbers |
| Use a journal format | `quarto use template quarto-journals/<journal>` | Reformatting by hand |
| Test the compendium | Fresh clone, `docker build`, `docker run` | Files that live only on your machine |
| Mark a milestone | `git tag -a v1.0-submission` | Not knowing what was submitted |

: Compendium tasks at a glance. {#tbl-zzcollab-cheat-sheet}

- [@marwick2018packaging], the paper that defines the research
  compendium as this chapter uses it, and whose framing every
  approach in the chapter inherits.
- [@marwick2018rrtools], the `rrtools` package and its
  documentation.
- [@harrell2025rworkflow], the closest peer treatment of what goes
  in the compendium's `analysis/` directory once it exists.
- [@wickham2023rpkgs], the `R Packages` book, for `roxygen2`
  documentation, `R CMD check`, and publishing a `pkgdown` site in

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-10}

1. A research compendium is a directory tree that bundles a
   study's code, data, and narrative in one place, with a
   standardized layout. The reader can rerun the analyses and
   regenerate the paper with a single command. Marwick et al.
   (2018) argue that the compendium is the appropriate unit of
   reproducible research in R. An `rrtools` compendium has three
   components: an R package backbone (`DESCRIPTION`, `R/`), which
   gives dependency declaration (`Imports:`); an `analysis/`
   directory for the data and the paper, which holds the study;
   and a Dockerfile which, with `renv.lock`, gives environment
   reproducibility. A regular R package exports functions for
   reuse by others and has no data or narrative; the compendium
   repurposes the package structure as infrastructure, not for
   distribution on CRAN.
2. The Five Pillars are: (1) a **Dockerfile** (captures the
   operating system and system libraries), (2) an **renv.lock**
   (captures R package versions), (3) an **.Rprofile** (activates
   renv and sets project-local R options), (4) **source code** (the
   actual analysis), and (5) **data** (raw and processed, or a
   documented access path when data cannot be shared). Each pillar
   captures a layer that the others do not, and removing any one
   leaves the analysis unreproducible. A project with only a
   committed `renv.lock` and a Dockerfile still has to pin the
   source code and the data (and, if it has no `.Rprofile`, its
   activation). The code is pinned when it is committed and the
   reported version tagged; the data, when the files are in the
   repository or a committed checksum manifest records them.
   Nobody notices their absence until a rerun gives a different
   answer, which is why the audit in @sec-zzcollab-audit checks
   for them explicitly.
3. A framework is worth adopting when many projects should look
   alike or the setup will be repeated often; for a single paper,
   assembling by hand or with `rrtools` is enough. Every framework
   writes the pillars once. Keeping them consistent afterwards
   (lockfile, Dockerfile tag, data manifest) is still yours, and
   the audit is how you check it. `zzcollab` *wraps* `renv` and
   Docker and *follows* `rrtools`'s layout without calling it.
